column3: Repeats the focus verse's full movement: every soul tastes death and returns to God.
Sets good and evil together, showing the human haste that can confuse their pursuit, though it does not name testing.
The retained V12 route is explicit contrast evidence and does not support the focus verse's testing claim.
Directly repeats universal death and extends it to full recompense at resurrection.
The immediately preceding verse denies bodily immortality, directly preparing the focus's universal mortality.
Shows a claimed escape from temptation becoming the very temptation fallen into.
Joins the taking of souls at death with their return to the Lord.
The public appearance of Ibrahim has no focused relation to mortality, testing, or return.
Good and adversity expose unstable worship, closely instantiating testing through contrasting conditions.
States that all who are on earth return to God.
Its fire-assay imagery supplies a close counterpart to the focus reading of trial as disclosure.
Recasts communal misfortune as a test rather than a curse carried by the messenger.
Explicitly joins the creation of death and life to testing people by their deeds.
The immediate continuation records the disbelievers' mocking response within the same warning sequence.
The prayer not to become a test for disbelievers gives a limited, differently directed use of fitnah.
Return to God and complete recompense for every soul closely develop the focus's final clause.
Ibrahim's prior sound judgment does not clarify the focus verse's mortality or testing.
The she-camel is explicitly sent as a communal test, though its object differs from good and evil generally.
Each soul is tested by what it sent ahead before all are returned to God.
Tasting one's fitnah in fire closely joins experiential tasting and trial.
Names the testing of Musa's people after his departure, without the focus's good-evil contrast.
God gives life and death, and to Him people return.
The immediate next verse answers impatient demand for signs within the same pericope.
Warns that defiance may bring fitnah, a narrower consequence than the focus's universal testing.
Pairs human desire for good with despair when evil touches him, but does not frame them as a test.
The bliss of those saved from the Fire does not develop the focus's stated movement.
Calls the angelic disclosure a test and distinguishes harm from benefit, though in a specific narrative setting.
God gives life and death, and the final destination is to Him.
Affirms power to revive the dead, supporting the mortality-to-return horizon indirectly.
Harun identifies the calf as a test and calls his people back to the Merciful.
Wealth and children are explicitly tests, showing that valued goods can assay allegiance.
The demand for the promised event continues the focus pericope's reckoning horizon.
Its use of fitnah concerns identifying the afflicted or deluded party, only distantly related to general trial.
All dominion belongs to God and all return to Him.
The local account of heedless listening supplies only broad pericope context.
It explicitly allows that delay and temporary enjoyment may be a test.
Contrasts the first tasted death with protected life beyond it, extending the mortality theme.
Names a good trial bestowed on believers, directly showing beneficent conditions as testing.
The prayer not to be made a test for oppressors is a limited parallel to fitnah.
Tasting a nearer punishment is intended to prompt return, connecting experiential consequence and turning back.
The immediate fire warning gives the threatened endpoint behind the local sequence.
States that people are tested repeatedly yet may fail to repent or take heed.
The tree is made a test for wrongdoers, though it does not specify the focus's good-evil polarity.
Yunus's prayer from darkness does not directly clarify mortality, testing, or return.
Worldly adornment is explicitly a test and is contrasted with better, more enduring provision.
Creation tests deeds and the verse also sets that test beside resurrection after death.
The image of unbelievers' works as scattered ash has no focused route to the verse's three movements.
Explicitly rejects the expectation that a profession of faith will go untested.
Pairs each soul's own earning with return to the Lord and disclosure of disputes.
The sudden arrival of the warning continues the focus pericope's announced endpoint.
Assuming that no test would come leads to blindness and deafness, making trial a disclosed moral condition.
Directly reverses human judgments of good and evil, closely illuminating their testing function.
The fire's altered effect belongs to a nearby narrative but does not itself state the focus's trial or return.
Solomon's explicit test and subsequent turning show a particular trial-response sequence.
Calls an apparent evil good and assigns each person what he earned, a partial good-evil and accountability parallel.
Mockery followed by its encompassing consequence continues the same local warning progression.
The vision and cursed tree are made a test that exposes and intensifies response.
Names evil in creation but gives no testing, death, or return relation.
The immediately prior cosmic-order verse offers only broad local context.
People are made a test for one another, with patience asked as the response.
Describes the events as signs and states that God was surely testing, without specifying their content.
The continuing warning about protection from the Merciful gives only indirect local context.
People are tested through one another, exposing status-based judgments about divine favor.
Names Ibrahim's sacrifice episode as a manifest test, a clear but specific instance.
The defeat of Ibrahim's plotters does not directly develop the focus verse.
Wealth and children are explicitly identified as a test alongside God's greater reward.
Enmity toward each prophet may form adversity, but the verse does not frame it as the focus's trial.
The channel resonance concerns another scene and offers no focused mortality or testing relation.
Testing distinguishes truthful from false claimants, directly expressing trial as disclosure.
God tests people so striving, patience, and reports become manifest.
The local denial of protective gods gives limited pericope context but not the focus's core movement.
Musa's killing, rescue, delay, and arrival are described as repeated testing in a formative narrative.
Denial that creation is futile is joined directly to return to God.
Ibrahim's resolve against idols does not clarify mortality, good and evil, or return.
Both hardship and granted favor become a test, especially exposing attribution of blessing.
The destruction of earlier peoples has no focused connection beyond incidental universal wording.
The cited channel is unrelated to the focus verse's mortality and trial themes.
Persecution of believers and its fire consequence give a severe, agent-directed use of fitnah.
The garden's yield and river do not by themselves supply a focused testing or return relation.
Long enjoyment and shrinking dominion continue the local challenge to presumed security and permanence.
Those tested, then emigrating, striving, and persevering show trial followed by faithful response.
Brief worldly enjoyment is followed by return to God and tasted punishment for disbelief.
The correction of the claim that the Merciful has a child does not develop the focus verse.
Satanic suggestion becomes a test that exposes diseased and hardened hearts.
Death inevitably meets those fleeing it, after which they return for disclosure of their deeds.
The channel relation concerns a distinct Mosaic waiting scene, not the focus's stated movement.
Dawud recognizes that he was tested and responds by seeking forgiveness and turning back.
Explicitly lists fear, hunger, and losses as trials and calls for patience.
The local revelation warning offers only broad continuation of the surrounding pericope.
Abundant provision is a test, while turning away leads to escalating punishment.
Inheritance allocations have no focused relation to mortality as universal test and return.
A witnessed death and restoration affirm divine power over life, indirectly supporting the return horizon.
A ruinous assumption about God does not specify testing through good and evil or return.
Household eating permissions and self-greetings are unrelated to the focus verse.
The woe against every lying sinner has no focused mortality, trial, or return connection.
The challenge to believe God's signs does not clarify the focus verse's stated movement.
The brothers' private deliberation and appeal to God's judgment use good only incidentally.
The claim of building as though immortal directly contrasts with the focus's denial of permanence.
The repeated challenge about favors does not develop mortality, testing, or return.
Every soul is held by what it earned, reinforcing individual accountability after the focus's tests.
Explicitly traces death, life, death again, revival, and final return to God.
Those struck by calamity affirm that they belong to God and return to Him.
Hardship, distress, and shaking test the believers before promised help arrives.
A small number persevere through the river test, showing trial through a permitted good.
God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, providing a boundary for the focus's testing theme.
No soul dies except by God's permission at an appointed term.
Believers are explicitly tested in their possessions and selves and called to patience.
Death overtakes people wherever they are, directly reinforcing universal mortality.
God tests communities through what He has given them, within a call to compete in good.
A reachable game is made an explicit test to reveal who fears God unseen.
God appoints a term for human life and a further fixed term with Him.
Differing ranks and what people are given are explicitly made a test.
Deliverance from Pharaoh is described as a great trial from the Lord.
Warns of a fitnah whose effects are not confined to wrongdoers, broadening the communal stakes of trial.
God tests before distinguishing those who strive and take no confidants apart from Him.
Wealth and children are a means by which God tests and afflicts people before death.
Harm and mercy both lie under God's disposal, clarifying the focus's paired conditions.
Mercy tasted after harm can expose despair and ingratitude.
Favor tasted after hardship can expose boastfulness and denial of prior adversity.
Death approaches from every side but is not attained, extending the mortality-and-punishment horizon.
God gives life and causes death and is the inheritor of all.
God tests people through their differing conditions and will disclose their disputes on the Day of Resurrection.
Earthly adornment is made a test to reveal whose deeds are best.
The sequence of birth, death, and resurrection gives a concise mortality-to-return counterpart.
Jesus likewise names the day of birth, death, and resurrection.
Human formation, death, and resurrection are set out as signs of the coming return.
Those who emigrate and are killed or die receive God's good provision, linking death to recompense.
God gives life, causes death, and then gives life again.
After death, people will be raised again.
The resurrection on the Day of Judgment completes the focus's return horizon.
At death, the wrongdoer asks to be returned, making the finality of death explicit.
A barrier remains until resurrection, sharply defining the interval after death.
Trust in the Living One who does not die forms a contrast to the focus's mortal human subjects.
Abraham names God as the One who causes him to die and then gives him life.
God brings living from dead and dead from living and revives the earth; people will likewise be brought forth.
The believers are explicitly tested and shaken severely.
The contrast of living and dead supports the focus's mortality horizon, though it is not a full return statement.
God gives life to the dead and records what people sent ahead and left behind.
The challenge about reviving decayed bones directly concerns life after death.
The Prophet and his opponents are all destined to die.
God takes souls at death and in sleep, retaining some and releasing others to an appointed term.
The trumpet brings death and then resurrection before the divine presence.
Those judged confess two deaths and two lives, recognizing their accountability.
God gives life and causes death, and His decree brings a matter into being.
Evil-doers are not to be treated like believers in life and death; judgment distinguishes their outcomes.
God tests some people through others, connecting conflict to disclosed response.
The agony of death arrives as the unavoidable reality people tried to evade.
God alone causes death and gives life.
God has decreed death and cannot be outstripped, while retaining power to replace and recreate.
To God belongs life and death and power over all things.
When a soul's appointed term comes, it cannot be deferred.
The soul's arrival at the throat culminates in being driven to the Lord.
Honor and provision are explicitly described as a human test.
Restriction of provision is likewise explicitly described as a human test.
The number of the Fire's keepers is made a test, exposing differing responses to revelation.
Guardians are commanded to test orphans before entrusting their property, a specific procedural use of trial.
Musa acknowledges that God tests whom He wills and guides whom He wills.
God tests people through good things and bad and states their hoped-for return, nearly restating the focus's central sequence.
A secure town is made to taste hunger and fear after rejecting blessings, showing adverse conditions as consequence.
Worldly adornment is identified as a test, against which enduring devotion is preferred.
Human persecution is misread as God's punishment, distinguishing pressure from the response it exposes.
The owners of the garden are explicitly tested through their provision and their intended response to it.
Human beings are created from a mixed drop in order to be tested.
